title: A holy quarrel
translation: Shōkū, a priest from Mount Kōya, was on his way to the capital. On a narrow path he met a woman on horseback. The man leading her horse was careless and sent the priest's horse into the ditch.

The priest was furious. "This is an outrage! Now listen. Of the four kinds of Buddhists, a nun is below a monk, a layman is below a nun, and a laywoman is below a layman. And a mere laywoman like you has a monk kicked into a ditch! A sin without precedent!"
"Sorry, sir, what was that?" said the man with the horse. "I didn't understand a word."

That made the priest even angrier. "What did you say? You ignorant, unschooled oaf!" he shouted. Then, with the look of a man who has just said something truly outrageous, he turned his horse round and hurried off.
A very holy quarrel, no doubt.

literal: When Holy Man Shōkū of Kōya was going up to the capital, on a narrow path a woman riding a horse met him, and the man leading (her horse) by the bit led it badly and made the holy man's horse fall into the ditch.
The holy man, very angrily, reproached them: 'This is an unheard-of outrage!
As for the four classes of disciples, listen: nuns are inferior to monks, laymen are inferior to nuns, and laywomen are inferior to laymen.
That one in the position of such a laywoman should have a monk kicked into a ditch is an evil deed never seen before', he said;
the man leading the horse said, 'What might you be saying? I cannot understand it at all',
(and) the holy man, still more enraged, said roughly, 'What do you say? You man of no practice and no learning!',
and with the look of one who thought he had said something extremely abusive, he turned his horse round and fled.
It must have been a venerable quarrel.

notes.text: {高野|かうや}: Mount Kōya, the great monastery of the Shingon school, south of Nara. Nothing certain is known about this Shōkū; he is probably not the well-known Pure Land teacher of the same name.
The man who walks in front of a horse and leads it by the bit. The woman is riding, and he is leading her horse.

The four classes of Buddhists: monks ({比丘|びく}), nuns ({比丘尼|びくに}), laymen ({優婆塞|うばそく}) and laywomen ({優婆夷|うばい}). The words are Sanskrit, written in Chinese characters for their sound (bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, upāsikā). The holy man shouts this at a man leading a horse.
え … ず: 'cannot'. こそ needs the realis form, so ず becomes ね. 'I can't understand it at all.' The polite question is the only thing he says.
'A man with no practice and no learning': a phrase for an ignorant monk. The priest throws it at a layman who never claimed to be either.

notes.quote: きはまりなき放言しつと思ひける気色にて
notes.text: {放言|はうげん}: abusive words, not modern 'careless remark'. {気色|けしき}: a look, an expression (not modern 'scenery'). The text does not say whether he was pleased with himself or ashamed; it only describes his face, and then he runs.

notes.quote: たふとかりける諍論なるべし
notes.text: たふとし: 'holy, venerable'. べし: 'surely, must be'. Kenkō's only comment. {諍論|いさかひ}: the reading is the 1925 edition's.
